body: I've converted DynamicSkipExample in the samples project to a PCL, and I'm able to repro this issue.
Interestingly, if I run the tests with `-noappdomain` in the console runner, they discover and run correctly. My guess is that the issue is related to remoting.

Okay, I've figured out the issue.

When you import the `xunit.core` namespace, it (purposefully) causes a copy of `xunit.execution.desktop` to be emitted into the bin folder on build, in addition to the expected `xunit.execution.dotnet` (which is what PCLs use). The runners are incorrectly guessing that these tests should be run in desktop mode, and running them with app domains turned on, which causes your custom test case not to be correctly remoted; since remoting is not available on PCLs, there's no way for you to "fix" this in your source.

The work around is to create a configuration file, and turn off app domain support. Choose one of these two methods (they both work with PCLs):
- [Configuring xUnit.net with JSON](http://xunit.github.io/docs/configuring-with-json.html)
- [Configuring xUnit.net with XML](http://xunit.github.io/docs/configuring-with-xml.html)

Thanks for the investigation, @bradwilson. The unfortunate thing in my case is I'm developing xunit.SkippableFact as a NuGet package for folks to consume. Now they have to manually create one of these files in order for the package to work. 
May I assume you're keeping this bug active to track removing the need for the workaround?
Yes, I'm looking into a fix.
Also, if you're designing this to be used by 3rd parties, you should ship both desktop and dotnet versions.
interesting idea... what would the difference be between the two, since everything I'm doing can be done in portable?

Users who write desktop unit tests will only ever link against `xunit.execution.desktop`, but your PCL links against `xunit.execution.dotnet`, so it's not usable in a desktop unit test (only in a PCL or a device unit test).

In practice, the source may be the same, but with two compiled outputs with different names, linked against each of the different execution libraries.
I see. So my source code will be the same, but the fact that it compiles under two projects will change xunit references. I can do that.
Right. :)

You'll need to create the two assemblies with the suffixes `.desktop.dll` and `.dotnet.dll`, and mark the assembly with `[assembly: PlatformSpecificAssembly]` so that the xUnit.net serialization system knows how to deal with anything that might get serialized from your assembly (like the test case).

The net effect when serializing type names is that it converts `MyAssembly.dotnet.dll` or `MyAssembly.desktop.dll` into `MyAssembly.{platform}.dll`, so that objects can be serialized in one space and deserialized in the other. This primarily affects the Visual Studio runner, which always uses the desktop DLLs to do discovery, but will use the dotnet DLLs when running the tests outside the desktop (phone & Windows store apps).

Name munging:

https://github.com/xunit/xunit/blob/e6894567a7d270e4eb34aad7ed81a8255740e464/src/common/SerializationHelper.cs#L230-L234 (serialization)
https://github.com/xunit/xunit/blob/e6894567a7d270e4eb34aad7ed81a8255740e464/src/common/SerializationHelper.cs#L155-L158 (deserialization)

You should also use the `.{Platform}` extension in your test case discovery declarations:

https://github.com/xunit/xunit/blob/e6894567a7d270e4eb34aad7ed81a8255740e464/src/xunit.core/FactAttribute.cs#L11

(This prevents you from having to have #if statements around the declaration for the different platforms... admittedly a bigger time saver when we had 7 platform DLLs rather than 2 :smiley:)

issue.title: Documentation: "How to write an extensibility point with xunit.execution to support both desktop and dotnet"

repository.name: xunit
repository.description: xUnit.net is a free, open source, community-focused unit testing tool for .NET.

body: The obvious fix here is to say "if I see both `xunit.execution.dotnet` and `xunit.execution.desktop` assemblies here, I should treat it as though it were a .dotnet library", since the reality is that that's the primary way you get into that situation. That has implications for people who build all binaries into a single folder, but breaking those people's assumptions doesn't particularly bug me that much (since they're wrong :stuck_out_tongue:).

@bradwilson I tried to follow all your steps above in Xunit.SkippableFact. But they still aren't being discovered. Could you take another peek at my updated attempt? 
https://github.com/AArnott/Xunit.SkippableFact/tree/iosSupport
You still have a dotnet-only assembly (`Xunit.SkippableFact`). You need to move all that code into the shared library, too.

Here's what I did:
- Upgrade the Visual Studio runner to 2.1 (required to run `dotnet` unit test projects)
- Move all the code out of `Xunit.SkippableFact` into the shared project
- Created a new test project (`Xunit.SkippableFact.Tests.Desktop`) which is a .NET 4.5.2 library, referencing `Xunit.SkippableFacts.Desktop`

Using the desktop unit tests, everything runs as expected with the existing 2.1 runners.

The portable unit tests still suffer from the problem that required the first for this issue, so using the console runner from the CI feed (`2.2.0-beta1-build3217`) allowed me to run the PCL unit tests correctly.

Note that the Visual Studio runner on the CI feed has not been updated yet, so it's still not capable of running these tests. Once it gets updated to use the latest xunit.runner.utility library, it too should be able to correctly discover and run those tests.

I believe that this is never going to run correctly inside of Visual Studio.

In order for these tests to run, they have to forego app domains. When you do that with the Visual Studio runner, you end up with DLLs staying locked inside the the `TE.ProcessHost.Managed.exe` process, which Visual Studio is using to do the discovery. When app domains are disable, the test assemblies are loaded directly into the app domain with the discovery process, which stays alive and therefore keeps the assemblies locked:

There's not much that can be done here for this I'm afraid. Unit testing PCL libraries in Visual Studio has always been a bit of a sketchy situation, if the tests can't directly run inside the desktop app domain model.

I can live with a more difficult test run for this project itself so long as consumers can do it easily enough.
I haven't read all your comments yet of what to try next so I'll get to that and reply more when it's done.

> I can live with a more difficult test run for this project itself so long as consumers can do it easily enough.

The Visual Studio issue affects everybody, not just you. The fact is that PCL-based unit tests just don't work as expected in Visual Studio, and never will. I'm going to drop "official" support for them, even though there's no technical way I can block them.
